title: Honey: Nature's Wonder Sugar
summary: Josh and Chuck explore honey: how bees make it (nectar, crop/honey stomach, regurgitation and enzymes, dehydration), honeydew honey, the history of beekeeping and skeps, and honey's sugar and compound makeup. They cover health claims (allergies and local honey, inflammation, wound healing, cancer, neurological effects, blood pressure), Manuka and jungle honey, heating and crystallization, grading (raw, filtered, ultra-filtered, pasteurized, diatomaceous earth, color scale, organic), monofloral vs multifloral flavors, and a celebrity honey venture. The episode ends with a listener mail message about a former English professor and a sign-off. Includes a soapbox segment on animal testing and a tangent on cocktails and Montenegro.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to honey
segments.summary: Hosts joke about a bad connection and talk about eating spun honey, then introduce the topic of honey and mention their earlier beekeeping episode.

segments.title: How bees make honey
segments.summary: Bees collect nectar and store it in their crop (honey stomach), mixing it with pollen, enzymes and moisture removal through regurgitation between bees until it becomes honey. Honey is described as a mixture of bee enzymes, nectar, and dehydrated compounds.

segments.title: Honeydew honey and the Western honeybee
segments.summary: Honeydew honey is made by bees from aphid-produced sap on plant stems, leaves and bark rather than from flowers. The hosts note that only some bee species make honey, with the Western honeybee being the main domesticated honey producer.

segments.title: History of beekeeping
segments.summary: Humans have collected honey since the Mesolithic period, and beekeeping is thought to date back about five thousand years, with evidence from Egypt, the Indus Valley, Mesopotamia and China. Early hives were clay pots or baskets, and the skep, a upturned basket cone, remains a symbol of the beehive.

segments.title: Composition and nutrients of honey
segments.summary: Honey is mostly sugar, mainly fructose and glucose with some complex sugars, plus amino acids (including all nine essential ones), enzymes, polyphenols and flavonoids. It is acidic and antibacterial, so it lasts a long time, and crystallized honey can be liquefied in warm water rather than on a stove.

segments.title: Honey and heating; animal testing soapbox
segments.summary: The hosts discuss mixed claims about heating honey, then Josh describes rodent restraint-stress studies used in honey research and voices opposition to animal testing. Chuck mentions a cocktail with Montenegro.

segments.title: Health benefits: allergies, inflammation, wounds, cancer, neurological and blood pressure
segments.summary: Studies suggest honey reduces allergy symptoms when local honey is eaten, reduces inflammation via flavonoids, and helps heal diabetic foot wounds. Preliminary research links honey to cancer cell death, dementia outcomes, and some blood pressure effects, with the hosts noting the need for more study. Eating about a tablespoon a day is suggested as a sugar swap.

segments.title: Manuka and jungle honey
segments.summary: Manuka honey, a monofloral New Zealand honey, is prized for its antimicrobial properties attributed to methylglyoxal and is expensive due to scarcity. Jungle honey from Malaysia is described as a rising alternative.

segments.title: Listener mail and sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts read a short listener mail about a former English professor who replied to the hosts and shared his book website. Sign-off follows.
